reviews.review:
Warranted Humanity is an ambitious game that suffers from a common malady of the first-time game developer:

Unconscious bias.

The developer insists that you can develop your own playstyle, but there's clearly one he already has in mind, and by "develop your own" he means "find the edges and corners of the intended route" and "figure out where the trap options are."

The other issue is that in a zombie game, a genre defined as much by improvisation and survivalism as gore and horror, you have essentially no room to deviate from the intended path. 
You are *intended* to grind up Lockpicking, Courage, and Strength before you go into town or collect Survivors, because the most consistent source of the Tools you need to actually support those survivors are locked cabinets. 
The lockpicking minigame is a moderately clever variation on the "realistic" school thereof, as opposed to Fallout and Skyrim's "find the correct angle." Find the stuck pin and then wiggle the tension selector around in the Sweet Spot until it sets, and then let go before it pops loose.
This is hampered by the fact that unless you grind up about 5% Lockpicking Bonus, you won't be able to let go of the arrow keys in time to keep the pins from resetting unless you have literal MLG reflexes.

Can you make a Mallet to replace the Fencing Maul so you can make the fence to make your Survivors less suicidal? 
No, ♥♥♥♥ you.

Can you drive nails with a river rock until you find a hammer?
No, ♥♥♥♥ you.

Can you dig holes with a digging stick until you find a shovel?
No, ♥♥♥♥ you.

Can you make a bow and arrow to defend yourself with from spitter zombies?
No, ♥♥♥♥ you.

Can you work leather with a knife instead of leatherworking shears?
No, ♥♥♥♥ you.


Combine this with a clunky, unintuitive Shelter/Settlement menu, and you have a tall hill for the would-be survivor to climb.


With that said, if you can tolerate these - having been warned ahead of time - then you've got an interesting game ahead of you; clearly inspired by The Last Stand Union City, and inarguably a labor of love.

The soundtrack is excellent; easily the best part of the game.

With that said, even as a diehard fan of the survival-crafting-with-zombies genre I found it deeply annoying.
